There will be no engagement or involvement in war," Lee said.Seoul weighs limited action around HormuzLee said South Korea nevertheless needed to carry out "the minimum level of activities" required to protect its citizens and the transportation route for crude oil in the region.South Korea's Cheonghae military unit, which operates in the area, has already expanded the scope of its mission to carry out such activities."It is true that we are reviewing and thinking about ways to strengthen (measures) on this," Lee said.The remarks come as countries assess how to protect shipping and energy supplies around the Strait of Hormuz, a major route for global oil transportation.Trump says Seoul rejected Iran requestLee's comments also come weeks after US President Donald Trump said he had asked South Korea to join Washington in the "Denuclearization of the Islamic Republic of Iran".Trump said in an August post on Truth Social that Lee had declined the request."While somewhat unrelated (?), I recently asked the President of South Korea if they would like to join us in the Denuclearization of the Islamic Republic of Iran, and they said, ‘No thanks!’ Thank you for your attention to this matter," Trump said.Trump also announced a substantial reduction in annual US-South Korea joint military exercises. He cited their cost, his "very good relationship" with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and concerns that the drills could send an "inappropriate and hostile" message to Pyongyang."Based on my very good relationship with Kim Jong Un, of North Korea, I was not happy with the fact that the United States had, long ago, agreed to participate in Joint Military Exercises with South Korea," Trump said.Lee rules out bid for another termLee also addressed domestic political speculation during the press conference, saying he would not seek another presidential term."I once again make it clear that I have no intention to seek reelection," he said.Lee said seeking reelection was also constitutionally impossible under the current system. The South Korean Constitution states that a constitutional change affecting the presidential system cannot apply to the president who is in office when the amendment is made.The remarks came after opposition parties repeatedly called on Lee to clarify his intentions, while accusing him of seeking a way to remain in power.Friday's event was Lee's seventh press conference since taking office in June 2025. Yonhap described it as unusual because his earlier press conferences were generally linked to occasions such as anniversaries of his administration.The press conference was announced three days earlier and came amid a recent decline in Lee's approval ratings, which have fallen into the mid-30 per cent range, particularly among younger voters, according to Yonhap.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Rewards for justice': US offers $15M for info on Iran's secretive financial networks
articles.summary: US News: The US department of state has offered a reward of up to $15 million for information that could help disrupt the financial mechanisms of Iran’s Islami.
articles.body: The US department of state has offered a reward of up to $15 million for information that could help disrupt the financial mechanisms of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and its various branches, including the IRGC-Qods Force (IRGC-QF).The Rewards for Justice programme is seeking information on how the IRGC raises, moves and transfers money, including through illicit financial schemes, front companies, financial institutions and other facilitators.The reward offer covers information on IRGC oil-for-money schemes, companies operating internationally on its behalf, entities helping it evade US and international sanctions, and financial institutions or exchange houses facilitating its transactions.The US is also seeking information on how the IRGC transfers funds and materials to groups it supports, as well as its donors, financial facilitators, businesses and investments. The offer includes information on front companies involved in procuring dual-use technology for the IRGC and criminal schemes that financially benefit the organisation.The state department said the IRGC, founded in 1979 following Iran's Islamic Revolution, is part of Iran's military. It said the IRGC-QF plays a central role in directing Iran's operations outside the country through groups including Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran-backed militia groups in Iraq. These are US government characterisations.The IRGC has been designated by the US as a foreign terrorist organisation since April 2019. The treasury department had previously designated it as a specially designated global terrorist in 2017.The reward comes as the US steps up efforts to target Iran's financial networks. On Thursday, the treasury department's office of foreign assets control sanctioned Iranian digital-asset exchange BitBank, its developer Pishtaz Simorgh Electronic Trade Company and three associates of Iranian financier Babak Zanjani.The treasury department alleged that BitBank had been used to transfer payments to the Iranian regime and said Zanjani had used the platform to facilitate the transfer of hundreds of millions of dollars in Bitcoin to the IRGC.The treasury action was part of what the administration calls Operation Economic Outcast, a campaign aimed at disrupting Iran's revenue sources and sanctions-evasion networks.The Rewards for Justice programme, administered by the state department's bureau of diplomatic security, offers financial rewards for information that can advance US national-security objectives, including disrupting the financial mechanisms of foreign terrorist organisations.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1992, a Maryland woman bought her aunt's old piano for $25; a stuck pedal revealed more than 100 baseball cards, and 27 years later a 1916 Babe Ruth rookie sold for $130,054
articles.summary: UK News: A $25 piano bought in Maryland in 1992 turned out to be hiding 112 baseball cards, including a 1916 Babe Ruth rookie card. The card was found inside a.
articles.body: A $25 piano bought in Maryland in 1992 turned out to be hiding 112 baseball cards, including a 1916 Babe Ruth rookie card. The card was found inside a stuck pedal and remained with the buyer for 27 years before being put up for auction. It eventually sold for $130,053, far above the expected price of $60,000 to $75,000.Ellen Kelly bought the old piano from a family estate sale in Westernport, Maryland, in 1992, Yahoo Sports reported. The piano had belonged to her aunt Nora, who had kept it at her home. Kelly said she never remembered it working, but she still wanted to play it after buying it for $25.That led to an unexpected discovery. When Kelly asked a friend to repair a pedal and tune the piano, the friend found that the pedal was stuck because 112 baseball cards had been placed inside it. As Kelly looked through the cards, she noticed one of the biggest names in baseball history. "He was looking at a pile of cards and I said, 'Hey, there's Babe Ruth,'" Kelly recalled.The cards were believed to have been placed inside the piano by Kelly's father or uncle. Kelly said they may have hidden them there because her aunt was a neat freak and might have thrown them away. The cards had apparently remained inside the piano for decades, with the Babe Ruth card among them.Babe Ruth card sells for $130,053The card found by Kelly was a 1916 Sporting News M101-4 Babe Ruth rookie card. It shows Ruth's photograph along with his name, position and team on the front, while the back is blank.The card was later included in the Beckett Goodwin Masterpieces and Uncommon Commons 78 auction. It attracted 23 bids before selling for $130,053. The auction result was around twice the amount expected before the sale."We were expecting $60,000-$75,000 for the card, so it far exceeded our expectations," said Steve Bloedow, Beckett Director of Auctions, in a Beckett news release.Bloedow also pointed to the condition and appearance of the card. "Ruth's RC continues to soar in price and has clearly joined the hobby's elite. The centering and eye appeal on this one was very strong so it's not shocking that it exceeded all expectations."The card received a BVG grade of 2.5, described as Good+. Despite that grade, its sale price made it notable among publicly sold cards in the same graded condition.A different Ruth rookie card had sold at Heritage Auctions in 2009 for $38,837. That card had received a grade of 6 on a scale of 10, which was higher than Kelly's card.Despite having the lower grade, Kelly's card sold for more than four times the 2009 price. Forbes reported that the earlier sale would be worth $46,017.44 in today's dollars after adjusting for inflation.What else did Kelly find?The Babe Ruth card was not the only baseball card Kelly found. The piano contained 112 cards in total, dating from 1916. Kelly's collection included cards featuring other Hall of Fame players from that period, including Walter Johnson and Grover Cleveland Alexander.The cards had remained inside the piano's pedal area for years. Their condition was described as surprisingly good by a senior grader who spoke to Sports Collectors Daily. However, the cards had dust stains and a crimp that was believed to have come from being stored underneath the pedal.Kelly eventually decided to sell the cards rather than continue keeping the collection. She said she wanted the money to help care for her brother's medical condition and to buy a new vehicle because her truck was breaking down.The Babe Ruth card was sold separately at auction, while the other 110 cards from 1916 were sold together. According to Forbes, that group fetched $4,420.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.body: Shopify cofounder and CEO Tobias Lütke has shifted his stance on workplace AI use, cautioning employees not to let the technology do all their work. According to a report by Fortune, speaking on The Knowledge Project podcast, Lütke said staff were producing unexamined emails and code with AI, creating what he called “slop grenades” that burden colleagues with cleanup. “You’re just letting AI do the work for you,” he warned, noting that AI should synthesize points in an email rather than generate long, sloppy missives.Researchers have coined the term workslop to describe polished-looking but low-value AI output that drags down productivity. A survey by BetterUp Labs and Stanford’s Social Media Lab found that over half of U.S. desk workers admitted to sending workslop, while 38% reported receiving it. On average, employees spent 3.4 hours per month revising AI-generated work, costing organizations millions in lost productivity.Duolingo's CEO tells a similar storyLütke isn't alone in reversing course. Duolingo CEO Luis von Ahn made headlines last year for declaring the company would go "AI-first" — a policy that tied employee evaluations to AI usage, replaced human contractors with AI tools, and limited headcount growth to only what automation couldn't handle. By May, though, Von Ahn was telling Fast Company he'd been swept up by how convincing AI-generated writing looked in demos, without accounting for how it holds up at scale compared to human creativity. He pointed to Duolingo's need to produce large volumes of story content for language lessons, estimating a meaningful share of AI-scaled output ends up being low-quality filler that has to be caught before it reaches users.The rise of 'workslop'Researchers now have a name for exactly what Lütke and Von Ahn are describing: workslop — AI-generated output that looks polished and complete on the surface but lacks the substance to actually be useful, forcing someone else to redo the work.A survey of 962 full-time American desk workers conducted this year by BetterUp Labs and Stanford's Social Media Lab found that more than half of respondents (52.7%) admitted to sending workslop to a colleague, a habit that showed up more often in workplaces that actively encouraged AI adoption. More than a third (38%) said they had been on the receiving end of it, spending an average of 3.4 hours a month cleaning it up. Common examples cited included emails with broken links or code that was needlessly overcomplicated.The damage isn't just measured in wasted hours. The survey found that workslop erodes trust between coworkers — recipients rated colleagues who sent it as less competent and less friendly, and more than a third of those who'd received it said they'd actively try to avoid working with that person again in the future.The cost is climbingThis year's findings mark a worsening trend compared to last year's version of the same survey, when 40% of respondents reported encountering workslop and said cleanup took roughly two hours on average. That earlier figure translated to about $186 in lost productivity per affected employee each month, or as much as $9 million annually in lost productivity for a 10,000-person organization — a number that's now almost certainly higher given this year's longer average cleanup time.Get the latest technology news and updates.
